learn: Why learn a policy directly instead of values
The policy objective, the log-derivative (score-function) trick and the policy gradient theorem
Natural gradients, TRPO and PPO's clipped objective
Continuous control: DDPG, TD3 and SAC
intro.why: Policy-gradient methods handle continuous actions and stochastic optimal policies naturally, and they are the family behind PPO, the workhorse of modern deep RL and of RLHF for language models.

sections.title: Value-based vs policy-based methods
sections.plain: Instead of learning values and acting greedily, learn the action probabilities themselves.
sections.body:
Value-based methods learn $Q$ and act (ε-)greedily; the policy is implicit. Policy-based methods parameterise the policy $\pi(a\mid s,\theta)$ and adjust θ by gradient ascent on performance.

Value-based (e.g. DQN)Policy-based (e.g. REINFORCE, PPO)
OutputQ-values; argmaxAction distribution
Continuous actionsHard (max over a continuum)Natural (e.g. Gaussian)
Stochastic optimal policiesCannot represent (only near-deterministic ε-greedy)Can
Policy changesCan jump abruptly when argmax flipsSmooth in θ (better convergence properties)
Sample efficiencyUsually better (off-policy replay)Often worse (high-variance, on-policy)
ConvergenceCan diverge with approximationTo a local optimum

When the best policy is stochastic: rock–paper–scissors (any deterministic policy is exploited), and state aliasing. Short corridor: three cells look identical, the middle one reverses actions; deterministic policies never reach the goal, while P(right) ≈ 0.59 achieves value ≈ −11.6 (ex1). A policy may also simply be easier to represent than a value function.

sections.title: Softmax and Gaussian policies
sections.plain: Discrete actions: softmax over preferences. Continuous actions: a Gaussian with learned mean and spread.
sections.body:
Softmax in action preferences (discrete actions):

$$\pi(a\mid s,\theta) = \frac{e^{h(s,a,\theta)}}{\sum_b e^{h(s,b,\theta)}},\qquad h(s,a,\theta) = \theta^\top\mathbf x(s,a),\qquad \nabla\ln\pi(a\mid s,\theta) = \mathbf x(s,a) - \sum_b\pi(b\mid s,\theta)\mathbf x(s,b)$$

Preferences can be driven toward a deterministic policy (unlike ε-greedy) or settle at any stochastic one. Preferences can be linear or a deep network.

Gaussian policy (continuous actions): $\pi(a\mid s,\theta) = \mathcal N\big(\mu(s,\theta), \sigma(s,\theta)^2\big)$, with σ often parameterised as $e^{\theta_\sigma^\top x(s)}$ to stay positive. $\partial\ln\pi/\partial\mu = (a-\mu)/\sigma^2$: actions that did well pull the mean toward them; the spread shrinks or grows depending on whether far-away actions helped.

sections.title: The objective and the policy gradient theorem
sections.plain: The gradient of performance can be estimated from samples without differentiating the environment.
sections.body:
Episodic objective: $J( heta) = v_{\pi_ heta}(s_0)$. Its gradient seems to depend on how θ changes the state distribution (an unknown property of the environment). The policy gradient theorem removes that dependence:

$$ abla J( heta) \propto \sum_s\mu(s)\sum_a q_\pi(s,a) abla\pi(a\mid s, heta) = \mathbb E_\pi ig[q_\pi(S_t,A_t)\, abla\ln\pi(A_t\mid S_t, heta) ig]$$

The second form uses the log-derivative (score-function) trick $ abla\pi = \pi abla\ln\pi$, turning a sum over actions into an expectation we can sample by following the policy. Intuition: increase the log-probability of each action in proportion to how good it was.

sections.title: REINFORCE
sections.plain: After each episode, make every action taken more likely in proportion to the return that followed it.
sections.body:
Replacing $q_\pi(S_t,A_t)$ by its unbiased Monte Carlo sample $G_t$ gives REINFORCE (Monte Carlo policy gradient):

$$\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t + \alpha\,\gamma^t G_t\,\nabla\ln\pi(A_t\mid S_t,\theta_t)$$

Worked. Two actions, softmax over preferences $\theta = [0.5, -0.2]$: $\pi = (0.668, 0.332)$. Action 1 is taken and the return is $G = 2$, $\alpha = 0.1$. Score $\nabla\ln\pi = [1,0] - [0.668, 0.332] = [0.332, -0.332]$. $\theta \leftarrow [0.5, -0.2] + 0.1\cdot2\cdot[0.332,-0.332] = [0.566, -0.266]$: action 1 became more likely.

REINFORCE is unbiased and converges to a local optimum under standard step-size conditions, but as a Monte Carlo method it has high variance and learns slowly; it must wait for episode ends.

sections.title: Baselines and the advantage
sections.plain: Compare each return with a typical return; only better-than-usual actions get reinforced.
sections.body:
Any baseline $b(s)$ that does not depend on the action can be subtracted without changing the expected gradient, because $\sum_a b(s) abla\pi(a\mid s) = b(s) abla\sum_a\pi(a\mid s) = b(s) abla1 = 0$:

$$ heta \leftarrow heta + \alpha ig(G_t - b(S_t) ig) abla\ln\pi(A_t\mid S_t, heta)$$

A natural choice is a learned state value $\hat v(S_t,\mathbf w)$; then $G_t - \hat v(S_t)$ estimates the advantage $A(s,a) = q(s,a) - v(s)$: how much better this action was than average. Variance drops sharply. On the short corridor (ex1, all returns negative) REINFORCE without a baseline needs α = 2×10⁻⁴; with a baseline α = 2×10⁻³ works, and episode lengths over the first 100 episodes fall from 29.7 to 17.8 steps on average.

sections.title: Actor–critic methods
sections.plain: A critic learns values; its TD error tells the actor whether an action was better or worse than expected.
sections.body:
Replace the Monte Carlo return by a bootstrapped one-step return, using a learned critic $\hat v(s,\mathbf w)$:

$$\delta_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma\hat v(S_{t+1},\mathbf w) - \hat v(S_t,\mathbf w),\qquad \mathbf w \leftarrow \mathbf w + \alpha_w\delta_t\nabla\hat v(S_t,\mathbf w),\qquad \theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha_\theta\delta_t\nabla\ln\pi(A_t\mid S_t,\theta)$$

δ is a low-variance (biased) estimate of the advantage. Actor–critic is fully online and incremental, and works in continuing tasks. On the corridor (ex2) one-step actor–critic averages 14.2 steps over the first 100 episodes and reaches P(right) ≈ 0.61.

Extensions: n-step returns and generalised advantage estimation (GAE) interpolate bias and variance; A2C/A3C run many environment copies (synchronously or asynchronously) for decorrelated data; entropy bonuses keep the policy exploring.

sections.title: Natural gradients, TRPO and PPO
sections.plain: Limit how far the policy can change in one update, measured in behaviour rather than in parameters.
sections.body:
A small step in parameter space can be a huge change in behaviour (and vice versa). The natural policy gradient preconditions by the Fisher information matrix $F$, so steps are measured by the change in the policy's distribution: $\Delta\theta \propto F^{-1}\nabla J$.

TRPO maximises a surrogate objective subject to a trust region on the average KL divergence:

$$\max_\theta\ \mathbb E\Big[\frac{\pi_\theta(a\mid s)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a\mid s)}A_t\Big]\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\mathbb E\big[\text{KL}(\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}\,\|\,\pi_\theta)\big]\le\delta$$

PPO gets a similar effect with a simple first-order clipped objective:

$$L^{\text{CLIP}}(\theta) = \mathbb E_t\Big[\min\big(r_t(\theta)A_t,\ \text{clip}(r_t(\theta),1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)A_t\big)\Big],\qquad r_t = \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_t\mid s_t)}$$

Worked. A good action ($A_t = +3$) whose probability rose so that $r_t = 1.3$, with ε = 0.2: clip(1.3) = 1.2; objective min(3.9, 3.6) = 3.6. The clipped branch wins and its gradient is zero: PPO refuses to over-commit to one sample. For negative advantages the cap applies below 1 − ε. The ratio is a one-step importance weight that lets PPO reuse a batch for several epochs.

sections.title: Continuous control: DDPG, TD3 and SAC
sections.plain: Off-policy actor–critic for continuous actions: deterministic actors, twin critics, or maximum entropy.
sections.body:
• DDPG: a deterministic actor $\mu_ heta(s)$ and a Q-critic; the actor follows $ abla_ heta J \approx \mathbb E[ abla_a Q(s,a)|_{a=\mu(s)} abla_ heta\mu_ heta(s)]$ (deterministic policy gradient); replay buffer and soft target networks as in DQN; exploration by adding noise to actions.
  • TD3: fixes DDPG's overestimation and brittleness with clipped double Q (min of two critics), delayed actor updates and target-policy smoothing (noise on target actions).
  • SAC: a stochastic actor maximising reward plus entropy, $J = \mathbb E[\sum_t r_t + \alpha\mathcal H(\pi(\cdot\mid s_t))]$, with twin critics and an automatically tuned temperature α; robust and sample-efficient.

All three are off-policy (replay), so far more sample-efficient than on-policy PPO, which matters for robots; PPO remains popular for its stability and simplicity, especially with cheap simulation.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• The score-function estimator is the same trick used for gradients through discrete sampling elsewhere in ML (e.g. variational inference with discrete latents).
  • Entropy bonus: adding β·H(π) to the objective prevents premature collapse to a deterministic policy.
  • Policy gradients and RLHF: PPO fine-tunes language models against a learned reward with a KL penalty (M12).
  • Local optima: policy gradients only guarantee a local optimum; initialisation and exploration matter.

code.title: REINFORCE on the short corridor, with and without a baseline
code.explain: Computes the exact value of the start state as a function of P(right) (best 0.585, −11.66), trains REINFORCE over 5 seeds with and without a learned baseline, and reproduces the worked update [0.566, −0.266].
mistakes: Forgetting that the score of a softmax is one-hot minus π.
Using the same step size with and without a baseline.
code.notes: With constant returns of one sign, the baseline is what lets the step size grow.
code.code:
"""REINFORCE on the short corridor with switched actions, with and without a baseline.

Four cells; start in cell 0, goal at cell 3; reward -1 per step. In cell 1 the actions are reversed.
All non-terminal cells look identical to the agent (state aliasing), so a policy is just
p = P(right). Any deterministic policy never reaches the goal; the best stochastic one does.
"""
import numpy as np
def J(p):                                  # exact value of the start state as a function of p (solve 3 linear equations)
    A = np.array([[1 - (1 - p), -p, 0], [-p, 1, -(1 - p)], [0, -(1 - p), 1]])
    b = -np.ones(3); return np.linalg.solve(A, b)[0]
ps = np.linspace(0.05, 0.95, 181); vals = [J(p) for p in ps]
best = ps[int(np.argmax(vals))]
print(f"best P(right) = {best:.3f}, value = {max(vals):.2f}; deterministic policies never finish; p=0.5 gives {J(0.5):.2f}")

def run(baseline, episodes=1000, alpha=2e-4, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed); th = np.array([-1.47, 1.47])     # start: P(right) ~ 0.05
    w, out = 0.0, []
    for ep in range(episodes):
        pi = np.exp(th - th.max()); pi /= pi.sum()
        s, traj = 0, []
        while s != 3 and len(traj) < 1000:
            a = int(rng.random() < pi[1])                                 # 1 = right
            move = (1 if a else -1) * (-1 if s == 1 else 1)
            traj.append(a); s = max(0, s + move)
        G = -np.arange(len(traj), 0, -1).astype(float)                    # return from each step, gamma = 1
        for t, a in enumerate(traj):
            grad = -pi.copy(); grad[a] += 1                               # grad log softmax = x(a) - sum pi x
            if baseline: d = G[t] - w; w += 0.02 * d
            else: d = G[t]
            th += alpha * d * grad
        out.append(len(traj))
    pi = np.exp(th - th.max()); pi /= pi.sum()
    return np.array(out), pi[1]
for bl, a in ((False, 2e-4), (True, 2e-3)):
    lens, p = zip(*[run(bl, alpha=a, seed=s) for s in range(5)])
    L = np.array(lens)
    print(f"REINFORCE {'with baseline' if bl else 'no baseline  '} (alpha={a}): mean episode length, eps 1-100: {L[:, :100].mean():6.1f}, "
          f"eps 901-1000: {L[:, -100:].mean():5.1f}; final P(right) = {np.round(p, 2)}")

# the worked update: theta = [0.5, -0.2], action 1 taken, G = 2, alpha = 0.1
th = np.array([0.5, -0.2]); pi = np.exp(th) / np.exp(th).sum()
score = np.array([1, 0]) - pi
print("\nworked: pi =", pi.round(3), " score =", score.round(3), " theta ->", (th + 0.1 * 2 * score).round(3))

REINFORCE with baseline (alpha=0.002): mean episode length, eps 1-100:   17.8, eps 901-1000:  11.9; final P(right) = [0.66 0.5  0.63 0.64 0.58]

code.title: One-step actor–critic and PPO's clipped objective
code.explain: Actor–critic on the corridor (critic sees cells; actor is aliased), then a table of clipped-surrogate values for several ratios and advantage signs, flagging when the gradient is zero.
mistakes: Applying the clip symmetrically regardless of the advantage sign.
code.notes: r = 1.3, A = 3 → 3.6 matches the worked example.
code.code:
"""One-step actor-critic on the same corridor, and PPO's clipped objective in numbers.

Actor: softmax policy (one preference per action, all cells aliased).
Critic: a separate value per cell (the critic is allowed to see the cell; the actor is not).
delta = R + gamma V(S') - V(S); critic V(S) += a_w delta; actor theta += a_th delta grad log pi(A).
"""
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
th, V = np.array([-1.47, 1.47]), np.zeros(4)
lens = []
for ep in range(1000):
    s, n = 0, 0
    while s != 3 and n < 1000:
        n += 1; pi = np.exp(th - th.max()); pi /= pi.sum()
        a = int(rng.random() < pi[1]); s2 = max(0, s + (1 if a else -1) * (-1 if s == 1 else 1))
        delta = -1 + (0 if s2 == 3 else V[s2]) - V[s]
        V[s] += 0.1 * delta
        g = -pi.copy(); g[a] += 1; th += 0.01 * delta * g
        s = s2
    lens.append(n)
pi = np.exp(th - th.max()); pi /= pi.sum()
print(f"actor-critic: mean length eps 1-100 {np.mean(lens[:100]):.1f}, eps 901-1000 {np.mean(lens[-100:]):.1f}; P(right) = {pi[1]:.2f}; critic V = {V.round(1)}")

print("\nPPO clipped surrogate  L = min(r*A, clip(r, 1-eps, 1+eps)*A), eps = 0.2")
print(f"{'r':>5}{'A':>5}{'r*A':>8}{'clipped*A':>11}{'L':>7}   gradient flows?")
for r, A in [(1.3, 3), (0.7, 3), (1.3, -3), (0.7, -3), (1.1, 3), (0.9, -3)]:
    c = np.clip(r, 0.8, 1.2); L = min(r * A, c * A)
    print(f"{r:5.1f}{A:5d}{r * A:8.2f}{c * A:11.2f}{L:7.2f}   {'no (clipped branch is active)' if L != r * A else 'yes'}")
